verses.text: “‘This is the law of the trespass offering. It is most holy.
In the place where they kill the burnt offering, he shall kill the trespass offering; and its blood he shall sprinkle around on the altar.
He shall offer all of its fat: the fat tail, and the fat that covers the innards,
and the two kidneys, and the fat that is on them, which is by the loins, and the cover on the liver, with the kidneys, shall he take away;
and the priest shall burn them on the altar for an offering made by fire to Yahweh: it is a trespass offering.
Every male among the priests may eat of it. It shall be eaten in a holy place. It is most holy.
“‘As is the sin offering, so is the trespass offering; there is one law for them. The priest who makes atonement with them shall have it.
The priest who offers any man’s burnt offering, even the priest shall have for himself the skin of the burnt offering which he has offered.
Every meal offering that is baked in the oven, and all that is dressed in the pan, and on the griddle, shall be the priest’s who offers it.
Every meal offering, mixed with oil or dry, belongs to all the sons of Aaron, one as well as another.
“‘This is the law of the sacrifice of peace offerings, which one shall offer to Yahweh.
If he offers it for a thanksgiving, then he shall offer with the sacrifice of thanksgiving unleavened cakes mixed with oil, and unleavened wafers anointed with oil, and cakes mixed with oil.
With cakes of leavened bread he shall offer his offering with the sacrifice of his peace offerings for thanksgiving.
Of it he shall offer one out of each offering for a heave offering to Yahweh. It shall be the priest’s who sprinkles the blood of the peace offerings.
The flesh of the sacrifice of his peace offerings for thanksgiving shall be eaten on the day of his offering. He shall not leave any of it until the morning.
“‘But if the sacrifice of his offering is a vow, or a freewill offering, it shall be eaten on the day that he offers his sacrifice; and on the next day what remains of it shall be eaten:
but what remains of the meat of the sacrifice on the third day shall be burned with fire.

If any of the meat of the sacrifice of his peace offerings is eaten on the third day, it will not be accepted, and it shall not be credited to him who offers it. It will be an abomination, and the soul who eats any of it will bear his iniquity.
“‘The meat that touches any unclean thing shall not be eaten. It shall be burned with fire. As for the meat, everyone who is clean may eat it;
but the soul who eats of the meat of the sacrifice of peace offerings, that belongs to Yahweh, having his uncleanness on him, that soul shall be cut off from his people.

When anyone touches any unclean thing, the uncleanness of man, or an unclean animal, or any unclean abomination, and eats some of the meat of the sacrifice of peace offerings, which belong to Yahweh, that soul shall be cut off from his people.’”
Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying,
“Speak to the children of Israel, saying, ‘You shall eat no fat, of bull, or sheep, or goat.
The fat of that which dies of itself, and the fat of that which is torn of animals, may be used for any other service, but you shall in no way eat of it.
For whoever eats the fat of the animal, of which men offer an offering made by fire to Yahweh, even the soul who eats it shall be cut off from his people.
You shall not eat any blood, whether it is of bird or of animal, in any of your dwellings.
Whoever it is who eats any blood, that soul shall be cut off from his people.’”
Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying,
“Speak to the children of Israel, saying, ‘He who offers the sacrifice of his peace offerings to Yahweh shall bring his offering to Yahweh out of the sacrifice of his peace offerings.
With his own hands he shall bring the offerings of Yahweh made by fire. He shall bring the fat with the breast, that the breast may be waved for a wave offering before Yahweh.
The priest shall burn the fat on the altar, but the breast shall be Aaron’s and his sons’.
The right thigh you shall give to the priest for a heave offering out of the sacrifices of your peace offerings.
He among the sons of Aaron who offers the blood of the peace offerings, and the fat, shall have the right thigh for a portion.

For the waved breast and the heaved thigh I have taken from the children of Israel out of the sacrifices of their peace offerings, and have given them to Aaron the priest and to his sons as their portion forever from the children of Israel.’”

This is the anointing portion of Aaron, and the anointing portion of his sons, out of the offerings of Yahweh made by fire, in the day when he presented them to minister to Yahweh in the priest’s office;
which Yahweh commanded to be given them of the children of Israel, in the day that he anointed them. It is their portion forever throughout their generations.
This is the law of the burnt offering, of the meal offering, and of the sin offering, and of the trespass offering, and of the consecration, and of the sacrifice of peace offerings;
which Yahweh commanded Moses in Mount Sinai, in the day that he commanded the children of Israel to offer their offerings to Yahweh, in the wilderness of Sinai.

footnotes.content: The trespass offering has a name—it's not hidden or unnamed. There's something comforting about that. When we've broken what was whole, God doesn't turn away; He names the remedy and makes a way back.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The place where the burnt offering is killed is already set apart as holy ground. Our offenses are brought to the same place where worship happens—God doesn't move the altar for our shame, we bring it to where grace is already at work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All the fat—the richest part—is offered. Not the scraps, but what's precious. That's what confession asks of us: the real, costly parts of our hearts, not performative leftovers.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The kidneys and liver, the seat of feeling and judgment—even what's hidden in us is brought to the fire. Nothing stays private when we seek true mending.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priest burns it for an offering made by fire. There's a physicality here that comforts me: real fire, real smoke, real presence. God doesn't deal with us in abstractions.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priests eat what's left, in a holy place. How tender: those who minister to the Lord's work are also sustained by it. Service and nourishment are woven together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One law for the sin offering and the trespass offering—the remedy for moral failure and the remedy for breaking what belonged to another follow the same path. The priest who brings both becomes one.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priest receives the skin of the burnt offering. Even in sacrifice, work is honored—the one who stands between heaven and earth doesn't do it for nothing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Every meal offering baked, dressed in a pan, on a griddle—the variety of preparation and the priest's provision are both real details. God cares that the worker eats.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One as well as another—the priests share equally, no hoarding. There's a kind order here that resists envy and greed, even in what's earned.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sacrifice of peace offerings—notice it comes with joy, not dread. The law itself opens a door for gratitude and wholeness, not just penalty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Thanksgiving cakes, unleavened and anointed with oil—the offerings are made with care, almost a feast. When we approach God to give thanks, He asks us to prepare something fine.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Leavened bread mixed with the unleavened—the two kinds together. Maybe it speaks to us bringing our whole selves, both the risen and the plain.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One out of each offering for a heave offering to Yahweh—the first fruits, the first portion. Generosity flows backward to God before it spreads anywhere else.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eaten on the day of offering, nothing left till morning—there's an immediacy and incompleteness to joy. We don't store it up; we taste it fresh, the way it's given.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Vow or freewill offering—both hold weight, though one is promised and one chosen freely. God honors both the oath we make and the gift we give because our heart moved us to.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: What remains on the third day is burned—decay breaks the sanctity. We can't pretend grace lasts forever just because we wish it. The third day matters.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eaten past the time, it becomes an abomination—not to God, but to the one eating it, who bears the weight of it. We can't steal what isn't ours to keep.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Meat that touches unclean things is burned—boundaries matter, not from cruelty, but from the nature of holiness itself. You can't blend the clean and unclean and call it whole.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The soul who eats uncleanly shall be cut off—separation is the consequence of willful mixing. Sometimes the price of ignoring the boundary is standing alone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Touching unclean things—from person, animal, or abomination—all defilement carries the same weight. The source doesn't matter as much as whether we acknowledge it and seek cleansing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying—the direct speech begins again. Every prohibition carries the weight of God's own voice, not human opinion.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You shall eat no fat of bull, sheep, or goat—the richest part belongs to the Lord's altar. What we hunger for most is often what we're called to surrender first.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fat from dead animals or torn prey may be used for service, but not eaten—the sacred and the practical are separated. Not all uses are equal, even if the thing seems the same.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Whoever eats forbidden fat shall be cut off—the penalty is stated clearly. God doesn't hide the cost of disobedience; He tells us plainly so we might choose wisely.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No blood, whether of bird or animal—blood carries life, and life belongs to the Giver. We're taught to honor the difference between what we eat and what we are.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The soul who eats blood shall be cut off—even the hidden sin of appetite has consequences. Nothing escapes notice when it touches the sacred.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying—His voice continues, patient and particular, teaching the people through laws that seem strange until we glimpse what they guard.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He who offers shall bring his offering with his own hands—the giver doesn't stand apart. What we offer, we must carry to the threshold ourselves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: With his own hands he brings the fat and the breast for a wave offering—the act is personal, visible, a movement before the Lord. No one can proxy true worship.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priest burns the fat, but the breast is Aaron's—the act of worship and the sustenance of the priesthood are both named and both honored.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The right thigh for a heave offering—specific, marked, distinguished. What we lift up to the Lord shapes what we're able to hold and carry forward.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priest who offers blood and fat receives the thigh—the one who stands in the gap is provided for, and the provision is public, not secret.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: I have given them to Aaron the priest and his sons as their portion forever—God's provision isn't temporary or conditional, but spoken as an eternal covenant.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This is the anointing portion, in the day when he presented them to minister—the priest's provision comes from the day of their calling, marking every meal as both work and grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Throughout their generations—the provision isn't given just once, but extended to sons and their sons. What the Lord establishes He sustains across time.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This is the law of the burnt offering, meal offering, sin offering, trespass offering, consecration, and peace offerings—all are named together, one system of how the broken approach the holy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this place-marking: Mount Sinai, the wilderness—when we feel far from home or cut off, remember that the laws of approach were given in a wilderness too. God's presence knew us even there.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
